extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, especially those studying Kantian ethics and its critics
extracted.subtask_description: A close critical examination of Kant's foundation for the moral law (the Categorical Imperative), Practical Reason, and related post-Kantian doctrines, arguing requirements and faults a satisfactory moral theory must satisfy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation must have real substance (not mere form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's foundation of the moral law is left with nothing but its Form (the abstract conception of lawfulness / universal validity); such pure a priori, abstract conceptions without real contents can never move men or have possible efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moral foundation should supply substantive content (real, empirical or motivating elements). Purely formal universality is insufficient to motivate actual human conduct; ethical theory must not 'float in the air' as a web of empty conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral claims cannot be asserted as facts of consciousness without empirical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law should not be presented as an empirically unexamined 'fact of consciousness' unless supported by evidence; to treat Autonomy or the Categorical Imperative as directly given in consciousness makes the claim anthropological/empirical and conflicts with Kant's repeated rejection of such grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one treats autonomy or moral duty as a fact of consciousness, this implies an empirical foundation and must be coherently defended; otherwise the move either commits petitio principii or contradicts one's stated methodological commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: A moral law's origin must account for motivating stimuli
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure of discovering or positing a moral law cannot plausibly occur purely a priori unless there is some antecedent moral stimulus; without a real, positive antecedent incentive, egoistic motives would remain the default guide for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical accounts must explain how moral motivation arises in agents — a theory that leaves motivation unexplained (or relies solely on abstract thought) fails to account for actual human conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular derivations (no petitio principii / 'absolute postulate')
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving the moral law by presupposing it (or by relying on an 'absolute Postulate') is a petitio principii: the doctrine assumes what it sets out to prove and so cannot provide a secure foundation for morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize derivations for hidden assumptions; calling a presupposed principle an 'absolute postulate' does not remove circularity. Fichte's and others' labeling of Kant's Categorical Imperative as an absolute postulate exemplifies this problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not posit Practical Reason as a mysterious special faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Reason is not a separate, occult 'qualitas occulta' or special moral instinct; rather, when reason performs the ratiocinative process Kant describes, it is the same faculty as Theoretical Reason exercising that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts that treat Practical Reason as a sui generis, metaphysically privileged organ (able to dictate 'ex cathedra') risk smuggling in dogmatic claims and undermining critical scrutiny; maintain parity between practical and theoretical reasoning faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent about freedom: don't both deny and postulate it without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant theoretically denies the possibility of freedom (holding determinism for human actions) but nevertheless postulates freedom as a practical requirement ('You can, because you ought'). Such inconsistency undermines the moral theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a theory denies freedom in its metaphysics, it cannot legitimately rely on freedom as a postulate to secure moral obligations; either the metaphysics or the practical postulates must be revised or justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making Reason an oracle that directly comprehends the supersensuous
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim that Vernunft (Reason) directly comprehends the Supersensuous (intellectual intuition of the Absolute, Divine, etc.) is unjustified and leads to mystification; such a stance produces divergent, incompatible metaphysical claims rather than shared, testable truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical method should resist deifying Reason as providing immediate, infallible metaphysical intuition; this temptation fosters dogmatic rhetoric and opens the door to contradictory religious and philosophical systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method must be honest and critical, not mystifying rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Kantian tendencies toward clap-trap, mystification, and asserting 'deliverances of Reason' without grounds amount to dishonest philosophizing; genuine philosophy should seek truth openly and make arguments accessible to scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rhetorical intimidation (portraying dissent as moral failure) or appeals to conscience to silence critique. The hallmark of sound philosophical work is transparent argumentation and genuine inquiry, not obfuscation or authoritative oracular claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify conceptual distinctions: reason (abstract concepts) vs understanding (intuitive perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason (Vernunft) properly denotes the capacity for abstract ideas, concepts and language-based thought, whereas the Understanding (Verstand, intellectus) is the faculty associated with intuitive perception and knowledge of causality (a priori forms enabling experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful conceptual taxonomy is required; conflating or redefining faculties to endow them with unwarranted powers (e.g., giving Reason intellectual intuition) invites confusion and poor argumentation. Definitions should align with historical and linguistic usage and with the explanatory role assigned them.
